name: gopus (pure-Go Opus codec)
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 (C reference encoder and decoder, SIMD build)
workload: Matched C and Go encode and decode workloads in ns per sample per channel: CELT fullband 20 ms stereo 128 kbps, CELT 5 ms mono 64 kbps, SILK wideband 20 ms mono 32 kbps, Hybrid fullband mono 64 kbps and stereo 96 kbps encode; decode of 20,075 RFC test-vector packets as float32 and int16.
claimed_speedup: Go SIMD takes 2.5-28.7% less time than matched C SIMD in four of five encoder cases (for example SILK wideband 329.21 vs 462.01 ns/sample, Hybrid fullband mono 225.80 vs 253.40, CELT fullband 20 ms stereo 126.28 vs 129.50) and 14.6% more in the 5 ms CELT case; float32 decode 33.14 vs 35.90 (7.7% less), int16 decode 37.64 vs 38.83 (3.1% less). Scalar rows: Go scalar is slower than C scalar in 6 of 7 rows (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.1 with GOAMD64=v3, GOEXPERIMENT=simd and PGO; C side GCC 13.3.0 with GOPUS_LIBOPUS_AMD64_TARGET=v3 (same x86-64-v3 target); each case three runs of at least 250 ms; reproduce with tools/encoderbenchcmp and tools/testvectorbenchcmp
tradeoffs: Go-only (no cgo) so C++ use needs an FFI shim or a Go service; the win needs GOAMD64=v3 and GOEXPERIMENT=simd, a Go 1.27 toolchain feature, and PGO; the README says the Go build tracks libopus 1.6.1 for bit-exact and quality parity, with optional DRED, QEXT and OSCE builds behind build tags.
caveats: First-party harness, but the comparison tools are public and the revision (candidate 4b660d668) and toolchains are named. Results are a mix: Go is slower in the scalar table and in one SIMD encoder case, and the faster rows are 3-29% rather than multiples. Measures codec work only, not file I/O. The README states its own file-based bench-encode and bench-decode examples include opus_demo process start-up in the C timings and are only rough. The repo shows 3,296 commits; the benchmarks were not run by this agent. The fork hujm2023/gopus (0 stars) shows older CI numbers where Go is 1.3-1.7x slower than libopus; those were not used.
found_via: WebSearch: 'pure Go Opus OR FLAC OR MP3 decoder faster than libopus OR libFLAC cgo benchmark github'; then opened thesyncim/gopus README (Performance section) and commits page

name: Falcon audio codec
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 (float and fixed point), opusfile 0.12, libvorbis 1.3.7, Tremor (decoders)
workload: Library-level single-thread decode of an 18-file 48 kHz stereo corpus (11 real recordings plus 7 synthetic signals) from memory to PCM in 20 ms reads, with Falcon and Opus files at equal size and Vorbis at its own quality setting; total times real time over the corpus, plus 256 simultaneous stereo voices.
claimed_speedup: Falcon 1114x real time vs libopus 1.6.1 float 731x (Falcon time 0.66x of libopus), libopus fixed point 629x, opusfile 717x, libvorbis 879x (0.79x), Tremor 877x (0.79x) on an x86-64 laptop performance core; Apple M5 1551x vs libopus float 1056x (0.68x) and libvorbis 1297x (0.84x). Faster than libopus on 18 of 18 files on both CPUs; stb_vorbis 1154x is on par on x86-64 and 1.28x faster on M5. 256 voices: 291 ms vs libopus float 365 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Falcon: Rust release profile, fat LTO, one codegen unit, x86-64-v3 on x86-64 (MSVC-toolchain DLL on Windows); C decoders built with -O3, GCC 15.1 (MinGW-w64) -march=x86-64-v3 on x86-64 and Apple clang 17 on M5; libopus with default SSE4.1/AVX2 runtime dispatch, stack protector off; best of two passes, at least 10 runs and 1 s per file
hardware: Intel Core Ultra 9 185H laptop (Windows 11, thread pinned to one performance, efficiency or low-power efficiency core) and a MacBook Pro with Apple M5 (macOS 26)
tradeoffs: A different codec, not a drop-in decoder for Opus streams: Falcon is an MDCT codec whose decoder is deliberately light and whose quality comes from encoder-side work. Uses more memory per stream than libopus (about 320-345 KB of heap per stereo stream plus a copy of the compressed file, vs 27 KB for libopus) and voice start-up is slower (156 us vs 46 us). Includes a C/C++ API (falcon_capi) with falcon.h and falcon.hpp. Quality claim is on par with Opus on an 18-file corpus, not an independent listening test. Version 2 was redesigned to avoid specific patents.
caveats: First-party numbers on one laptop CPU and one Apple CPU. The C comparison program that links all decoders was not found in the repo (tools/ holds only eval and quality; falcon_capi/examples hold decode examples), so the table cannot be reproduced from the repo as far as opened. The README says earlier versions compared against FFmpeg's built-in Opus and Vorbis decoders by mistake and withdrew the old Vorbis figures; against FFmpeg's Vorbis decoder Falcon wins only 5 of 18 files. Raw libopus is fed pre-extracted packets (no Ogg parsing) while opusfile, vorbisfile and stb_vorbis include container parsing. Falcon is Opus-class quality at equal size per its own metrics, but speed compares a different codec at the same file size, not the same bitstream.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/audio-codec?l=rust (description: beats Opus on quality at equal file size); opened README (Decode speed section, 'How this was measured'), repo page, tools and falcon_capi trees, commits page

name: rusty_h265
baseline: FFmpeg 8.1.2 native hevc decoder (libavcodec, hand-written assembly)
workload: Single-core pinned decode time of four HEVC test streams (720p 8-bit mainstream inter, 720p 10-bit, deblocking-heavy, weighted prediction), ABBA-alternated, 21 pairs, decoder-reported internal decode time (FFmpeg -benchmark rtime), frame counts checked.
claimed_speedup: Weighted-prediction stream 703 ms vs FFmpeg 741 ms (1.05x faster, 21/21 pairs, z = +4.58); deblocking-heavy 744 vs 675 ms (0.91x, FFmpeg faster); mainstream 720p 8-bit 447 vs 267 ms (0.60x); 10-bit 445 vs 308 ms (0.69x). The README itself says between 1.05x faster and 1.67x slower than FFmpeg. FFmpeg measured against itself: 0.992x. Release 0.6.0 is 1.08-1.16x faster than 0.5.0.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in README; builds target x86-64-v3 (AVX2) via tools/build-v3.sh; benchmark script tools/bench/codec-bench.ps1 (PowerShell, pinned to one core at High priority)
stars_or_usage: 2 stars; a commit message says 561 active installs
tradeoffs: Pure-Rust HEVC decoder with #![forbid(unsafe_code)] in the core and SIMD kernels isolated in rusty_h265-accel; decodes all 147 JCT-VC HEVC_v1 conformance streams byte-exact. Rust only, no stated C API; decoder only. Part of the Remade With Rust effort and the HEVC decoder inside remade_ffmpeg_rs.
caveats: Faster than FFmpeg on one stream out of four only, and by 5%; slower on the other three, so this is a flagged partial win. CPU model and compiler version are not stated; the weighted-prediction stream is a niche content type. Numbers are first-party; the harness script exists in the repo but was not run. The README says its own earlier 0.5.0 numbers did not match a re-measurement.
found_via: Opened Remade-With-Rust/rusty_h265 after the earlier wave 10 searches recorded remade_ffmpeg_rs (rusty_h265 was on the skipped list); README performance table and commits page

name: rav1d-safe
baseline: upstream rav1d (the Rust port of dav1d) built without assembly; against dav1d-derived assembly builds it is slower
workload: Still-image AV1 decode (12 inputs: photo and map at 1920x1080, 3840x2160, 7680x4320, minimum tiling and eight tiles, 8-bit 4:2:0 IVF) with 1, 4 and 8 workers; median of five paired repetitions per cell, geometric mean across inputs, MD5-checked against upstream and dav1d 1.5.3.
claimed_speedup: Checked rav1d-safe takes 0.680x the time of upstream rav1d without assembly with 1 worker (32.0% less decode time), 0.821x with 4 workers and 0.813x with 8 workers; for example photo-8k-min 231.4 ms vs 451.9 ms (0.512x). Against upstream rav1d with assembly the same page set shows checked rav1d-safe taking 1.8-8.6 times as long, and its README reports about 1.5x slower than the assembly build on 4K and 8K AVIF stills.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.98.1 (LLVM 22.1.8), release, fat LTO, one codegen unit, unwind panics, RUSTFLAGS=-C llvm-args=-align-all-functions=4; upstream rav1d commit d3d1cd6 with default-features=false (bitdepth_8, bitdepth_16); rav1d-safe commit be5b244 checked features (no unchecked, c-ffi, asm)
license: BSD-2-Clause AND AGPL-3.0 (commercial licence also offered), per the GitHub licence panel
tradeoffs: Memory-safe AV1 decoder: replaces about 160,000 lines of assembly with checked safe Rust SIMD under forbid(unsafe_code), native Rust API (C API behind an optional c-ffi feature that implies unchecked). Strict mode by default rejects non-conforming streams that dav1d conceals. Fork of rav1d, which is a port of dav1d.
caveats: Not faster than dav1d or assembly-enabled rav1d: the author's own pages say 1.5-1.6x slower on stills and 1.8-8.6x slower in the 2026-09-07 assembly comparison (video, frame threading not enabled). The win is only against upstream rav1d with its assembly turned off (which still contains unsafe Rust), and it is on still-image fixtures from a two-source seed corpus; the page says this is not an ablation of SIMD and does not establish parity. Map-content cells are near 1.0x (up to 1.002x at 4K, 4 workers, eight tiles). Dual AGPL/commercial licensing may restrict reuse. The baseline is not in the FFmpeg, x264, Opus list.
found_via: Opened imazen/rav1d-safe (on the skipped list of earlier searches); README Performance section, benchmarks/noasm-2026-09-08 and benchmarks/upstream-2026-09-07 pages, commits page

name: python-soxr
language: Python (wrapper over libsoxr in C, with a patched libsoxr copy)
baseline: libsamplerate (via the Python samplerate package, sinc_medium and sinc_best), also resampy, scipy.signal.resample, torchaudio
workload: Downsampling 10 seconds of 48,000 Hz audio to 44,100 Hz, CPU time in ms, run on Google Colab.
claimed_speedup: soxr (HQ) 10.8 ms and soxr (VHQ) 14.5 ms vs samplerate (libsamplerate) sinc_medium 223 ms and sinc_best 794 ms (about 21x and 74x, derived from page data for HQ vs medium and best); also vs resampy kaiser_fast 108 ms, resampy kaiser_best 310 ms, scipy.signal.resample 21.3 ms, torchaudio 13.8 ms.
stars_or_usage: 114 stars, 11 forks; on PyPI as soxr
tradeoffs: Python binding of libsoxr (already catalogued as chirlu/soxr), so the speed is libsoxr's; the package ships a patched libsoxr and the patch does not apply to dynamically linked (conda-forge) builds. LGPL licence. Streaming API (ResampleStream) and one-shot API. Quality settings differ between libraries, so the table compares speed at named quality presets, not equal quality.
caveats: The speed table is a summary of a Colab notebook that was not opened (colab.research.google.com is not reachable and the notebook link is only in the README); no CPU model, library versions or flags are given. The 'samplerate' row is the Python package of that name, which is a libsamplerate binding (inferred from the name; the README does not say so). Wrapper of an already-listed project, so it is likely a duplicate of libsoxr and is recorded mainly for the Python versus libsamplerate comparison. A comparison with the C libsamplerate through its Python binding adds binding overhead for the baseline.
found_via: WebSearch: 'audio resampler faster than libsamplerate OR libsoxr benchmark Rust OR Zig OR Go OR Python github'; opened dofuuz/python-soxr README (Benchmark section), repo page and commits page

name: ropus (Rust port of libopus)
baseline: libopus 1.5.2 (C reference, with its hand-tuned SSE4.1/AVX2 dispatch)
workload: Encode and decode time ratio Rust over C on ten WAV vectors (SILK narrowband and wideband noise, Hybrid noise, CELT noise, sine, sweep, square, TTS speech, stereo music), harness amortising codec construction, medians of five sweeps (tools/bench_sweep.sh --iters=30).
claimed_speedup: x86-64 ratios Rust/C (below 1.0 means Rust faster): encode SILK NB noise 0.97x, SILK WB noise 0.96x, Hybrid noise 0.97x, CELT sweep 0.96x; decode CELT square 0.92x, SILK NB 0.95x, CELT FB mono noise 0.98x, CELT sine 0.99x; means 1.06x encode and 1.01x decode (slightly slower overall). The README says Rust encode is faster than C on five vectors and decode faster or at parity on six.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler version and C flags not stated in the README; Rust build targets x86-64-v3 (AVX2, FMA3, BMI1/2) per the README CPU-target note; harness is tools/bench_sweep.sh driving the ropus-compare binary
hardware: Intel i7-14700KF under WSL2 (x86-64 table); Apple M1 Pro (second table, where decode is slower, for example SILK NB 1.30x and SILK WB 1.50x); earlier Ryzen 9 9950X3D baseline kept in a journal
license: BSD-3-Clause (the repo LICENSE is the upstream Xiph libopus licence text; the README says to refer to the upstream project licence)
tradeoffs: Rust port of libopus 1.5.2 including DNN features (LPCNet, FARGAN, DRED) with a C ABI shim (capi/) that exposes the libopus API, plus a differential FFI harness that compares byte-for-byte against the C reference; builds the C reference from a pinned xiph/opus checkout. Larger binary because of an embedded 8.78 MB weights blob.
caveats: Parity rather than a win: mean encode ratio is 1.06x (slower) and mean decode 1.01x on x86-64, and decode is 1.3-1.5x slower on some Apple M1 Pro rows. The README says earlier runs measured decoder construction cost, not steady-state decode. Single desktop CPU, compiler flags not given, first-party. The repo carries CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md (AI-assisted). Recorded because a few vectors are faster than the C baseline; the honest summary is roughly equal speed.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/audio-codec?l=rust; opened 0x4D44/ropus README (Performance section), LICENSE, tools/bench_sweep.sh, commits page

name: flacenc-rs
baseline: FLAC reference encoder (libFLAC flac tool, opt8, opt8lax and opt5 settings)
workload: Auto-generated encoder comparison report: average compression rate and average compression speed (inverse real-time factor) over four Wikimedia recordings, for the reference flac encoder at three settings and flacenc configurations default (multi-threaded), mt1, st (single thread) and experimental.
claimed_speedup: Nightly report (portable SIMD): flacenc st 331.5x real time and default (multi-threaded) 1309.5x vs flac opt8 229.7x and opt5 550.4x, at compression rate 0.5276 vs 0.5256 (opt8) and 0.5328 (opt5). Stable-toolchain report: st 126.5x, mt1 131.2x and default 575.3x vs opt8 230.9x and opt5 572.1x. Single-thread stable is slower than flac opt8.
compiler_and_flags: Nightly report uses the simd-nightly feature (rust portable_simd); stable report uses a fake portable_simd; Rust version and C flags not stated in the report
tradeoffs: FLAC encoder library designed for hackability, with an optional (experimental) decoder; the speed requires either nightly Rust with portable_simd or multi-threaded encoding (par feature, default on). Compression is about 0.4% larger than flac -8 (rate 0.5276 vs 0.5256).
caveats: The report does not state hardware, compiler versions or the flac version; the machine setting changed in a later commit ('Update benchmark results with new machine setting'). The multi-threaded default beats flac only by using several cores against the single-threaded flac tool; on stable Rust single-threaded flacenc is slower than flac -8 (126x vs 231x). Four short recordings only. The README makes no explicit speed claim and only links the report; the report was read from the checked-in markdown.
found_via: Named from my own knowledge of Rust FLAC encoders (not surfaced by a search); opened yotarok/flacenc-rs README, report/report.stable.md and report/report.nightly.md, repo and commits pages

name: rivet-h26x (rivet-h26x-codecs)
baseline: libavcodec (FFmpeg) native H.264 and H.265 decoders
workload: Decode of 720p Big Buck Bunny encodes (cabac3.264 H.264 723 frames, a CAVLC H.264 clip, hevc6.265 and wpp10.265 H.265 1200 frames), process-tree CPU seconds and frames per wall second, 1 thread pinned to one core and all threads, best of five, both decoders materialising every frame.
claimed_speedup: All threads on the wavefront H.265 clip wpp10.265: 1963 fps vs libavcodec 1774 fps (+10.7%); single-thread on that clip 1.938 CPU s vs 1.906 s (1.02x libavcodec's time, parity). Non-wavefront H.265 hevc6.265 all threads 1288 vs 1387 fps (-7.1%), single-thread 1.12x libavcodec's CPU time. H.264 single-thread costs 1.46-1.55x libavcodec's CPU time; H.264 all-thread fps 2169 vs 2119 (CABAC) and 3116 vs 3063 (CAVLC) are +2.4% and +1.7%, which the README says are within its 4% noise floor.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for either decoder; libavcodec version not stated; SIMD rungs selected at run time (AVX-512 tier on this CPU), regenerate with tools/benchmark.py (which no longer runs FFmpeg)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X 16-Core Processor, 32 hardware threads, AVX-512 rung, machine 17% busy before the run; single-thread rows pinned to core 29
license: Open Encoding Attribution License v1.0 (source-available, royalty-free with commercial attribution; not OSI-approved; no SPDX id confirmed)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; crates.io rivet-h26x 0.2; 515 commits; moved from the rivet-transcoder organisation to safewords on 2026-10-03
tradeoffs: Pure-Rust H.264 and H.265 decoders (no C, no build script, one dependency) with frame and wavefront threading and a run-time SSE2-to-AVX-512 and NEON kernel ladder; bit-exact on 204 JVT and 196 JCT-VC conformance streams; also an in-progress encoder. Source-available licence with an attribution requirement, so it is not freely copyable under an OSI licence.
caveats: A win in one cell of four: only the all-threads wavefront H.265 clip is ahead; single-threaded H.265 is at parity (1.02x and 1.12x libavcodec's CPU time) and H.264 is slower. The README says the ratio column is good to about +-5% between sessions and that the earlier table put wpp10.265 at 0.96x before an unchanged-code re-run gave 1.02x. The libavcodec rows are a 2026-09 record, since the tooling no longer runs FFmpeg. Whether libavcodec was pinned to equal threads on the all-threads rows is not stated beyond 'every thread'. Not run by this agent.
